summary:
Peru does not criminalise consensual same-sex sexual activity or trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. Ica stands under this national framework.

On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody, medical attention, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport. On 2 April 2025 the Plenary approved and exempted from second vote the bill, whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex' save for the listed exceptions. Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, codifies the restriction and also bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

Law 32331 also bars trans people from using public restrooms according to their gender identity, a state-imposed limit on daily movement that can intensify hostile interactions in transit spaces. The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of 15 April 2025, argues the law violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that its stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. The institute also invokes Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights, and records dehumanising comparisons made by congressman Lizarzaburu on the floor.

LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warns that bathroom access under the measure would depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents extends the restriction. Human Rights Watch reports that it mandates public-restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their identity; that its vaguely worded child-protection articles, notably Article 4 on media and advertising and Article 5, enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content; and that the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years. Human Rights Watch characterises child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Legal protection against discrimination and hate crime on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is absent. Government Decree Nº 1323 criminalised such discrimination with effect from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code; Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, President Kuczynski's veto stood at that point, and the protections were subsequently removed as the Penal Code was reworked. Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage.

Violence against trans people is rising and recorded figures understate it. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, covered by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023 (12 trans women) from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with multiple gunshots or stabbings. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denuncias in 2020. The report also recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. Co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender and journalist, states the recorded numbers are only a sub-registry. A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence.

The torture and rape of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, ended in conviction on 15 December 2025: police officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León received 17 years' imprisonment, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It is Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Legal recognition of gender is partially available. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Healthcare classifications have shifted in both directions. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, MINSA revised the term to 'gender discordance' in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients. Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with direct bearing on trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

Hostility is also institutional. Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional; and an April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order and security' grounds, which risks being weaponised against queer organising. In April 2025 the television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed the first openly-lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.
tangentialFactors:
The bathroom legislation's stated trigger, a July 2023 social-media complaint about restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport in Lima, indicates that ordinary visibility of trans-inclusive signage can prompt national restrictive legislation, a pattern relevant to any visitor expecting to encounter inclusive facilities elsewhere in Peru.

Gianna Camacho's warning that enforcement would rest on security staff's personal judgment, including demands for ID, means the practical burden of Law 32331 falls on front-line private and state security personnel rather than on a uniform legal test, introducing unpredictability into everyday transit spaces such as malls, transport hubs and hotels.

Peru's position as one of only three South American countries, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage places the country at the restrictive end of its regional comparators, and neighbouring jurisdictions may offer stronger formal protections than Peru does.

The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI figures cover Peru as a whole rather than Ica specifically, so the recorded homicide and violation counts describe the national environment a visitor enters rather than a local Ica rate.

The Azul Rojas Marín conviction, reached through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and decided by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, shows that regional human-rights machinery remains a functioning avenue for redress where domestic institutions fail, a channel also available to visitors who are victims of discrimination-based violence.

outOfScopeNotes:
Ica has no recorded trans-specific regional law, ordinance or departmental decree in the source inventory; the applicable rules are national. Whether Ica municipal authorities or private venues enforce Law 32331 more or less strictly than Lima is not sourced and remains unresolved.

The source inventory does not state whether the pending Gender Identity Law introduced 4 November 2016 has advanced after March 2021, nor whether any subsequent legislative session has acted on it; the current status is unresolved.

Whether the July 2025 Lima constitutional court decision striking an anti-equality decree has been appealed, or has effect beyond Lima, is not sourced here.

No Ica-specific data on reported violence against trans people, police conduct, or access to trans-competent healthcare appears in the inventory; the homicide and violation figures cover Peru nationally, and the sex-work prevalence study covers Lima and Callao.

The inventory does not resolve whether Law 32331 and the April 2025 child-sexual-integrity law have been challenged before the Constitutional Court, or whether any interim suspension is in force.
